title: Gravity, satellites and curved space
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 5 Physics: gravity, normal forces and applied forces; gravity and satellites. Goes further into weight on other worlds, tides, Lagrange points, curved space-time and gravitational waves, built on the DeepKids founder's gravity notes. No textbook needed.
summary: Two years ago your child found that everything pulls everything, that the ground holds us with a push back and that astronauts float because they are falling. Now they use those ideas like a physicist. They name gravity, normal and applied forces in full force diagrams, calculate their weight on the Moon, Mars and Jupiter, find out why gravity weakens with distance and vanishes at the Earth's centre, follow Newton's cannonball into orbit, meet India's satellites and the spacecraft parked at a Lagrange point, explain why the sea has two bulges, and go beyond Newton to Einstein's curved space-time, bending light, slower clocks and ripples in space heard in 2015.
builds_on: Gravity Class 3: everything pulls everything; bigger mass, bigger pull; further, weaker; the normal force from atoms pushing back; a scale measures the push back; free fall and floating astronauts; the space blanket; the Lagrange still point; centre of gravity; tides. Forces Classes 1–5: pushes and pulls, newtons, mass and weight, friction, upthrust, and this year force diagrams with resultant forces, air resistance and rockets. Later: in middle school, Newton's law of gravitation with numbers, and energy.
subconcepts: gravity, normal force and applied force in force diagrams
the normal force can be bigger or smaller than your weight (jumping, lifts, trampolines)
mass and weight on other worlds: newtons per kilogram
gravity weakens with the square of distance
inside the Earth gravity gets weaker, reaching zero at the centre
gravity is a little different from place to place on Earth
Newton's cannonball: how an orbit works
artificial satellites and what they do, including India's
tides: two bulges, spring and neap tides, and the Moon's locked face
Einstein's curved space-time: falling as following the curve
gravity bends light and slows clocks (eclipses and GPS)
dark matter: the invisible mass that gravity reveals
goals: By the end your child can draw force diagrams naming gravity, normal and applied forces, and explain when the normal force is bigger or smaller than the weight.
By the end your child can calculate their weight on the Moon, Mars and Jupiter, and explain why weight changes but mass doesn't.
By the end your child can explain an orbit with Newton's cannonball, and say why satellites need to go so fast.
By the end your child can name four jobs satellites do, and describe one Indian mission.
By the end your child can explain why most coasts have two high tides a day.
By the end your child can describe Einstein's idea of curved space-time and give one piece of evidence for it, and name scientists whose gravity work was doubted or overlooked.
words: gravity
the pull between all masses; in Einstein's view, things falling along curved space-time
normal force
the push of a surface back on whatever presses on it, at right angles to the surface
applied force
a push or pull that a person or thing gives directly
N/kg (newtons per kilogram)
how hard a planet pulls each kilogram: about 9.8 on Earth, 1.6 on the Moon
orbit
the curved path of something falling round a bigger body and always missing it
satellite
anything that orbits a planet; the Moon is natural, the ones we launch are artificial
escape speed
the speed you'd need to leave a planet's gravity for good: about 11.2 km per second for the Earth
Lagrange point
a place where the pulls of two big bodies and the motion of orbiting balance out
tide
the rise and fall of the sea caused by the Moon's and Sun's gravity
space-time
space and time together, which Einstein showed can be curved by mass and energy
gravitational wave
a ripple in space-time, made by huge masses moving very fast
dark matter
matter we can't see but whose gravity we can detect

days.title: Three forces in a game of gully cricket
days.goal: Recall what we learned about gravity in Class 3, hear the story, and name gravity, normal and applied forces.

steps.title: Back to the dust
steps.do: Remind your child of the Class 3 story about the dust that fell for four billion years. Ask: 'Who pulls whom?' (Everything pulls everything.) 'Why don't you sink into the floor?' (The floor's atoms push back: the normal force.) 'Why do astronauts float?' (They are falling with their station; nothing pushes on them.) 'Is anybody actually pulling?' (No; mass bends space and things fall along the bend.) Praise nothing; just ask what they still remember and what they now wonder.

steps.title: Story: The Moon Is Falling Too
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'What did the young scientist mean when he said the Moon is falling?' and 'Who knew about the Moon first, the scientists or Mary's mother?'

steps.title: Forces in gully cricket
steps.do: Play five minutes of gully cricket or catch. Then stop at moments and name the forces: the bowler's hand pushing the ball (an applied force); the ball in the air (gravity down, air resistance back); the ball hitting the pitch (the ground's normal force pushing up and bouncing it); the bat (an applied force); the batter standing (gravity down, normal force up). Ask: 'Which forces need touching and which don't?' (Gravity works at a distance; the normal and applied forces need contact.)

steps.title: First force diagrams
steps.do: Draw three pictures and add labelled arrows, longer for bigger forces: the batter standing still (gravity and normal force, equal); the ball flying (gravity, air resistance); a book you push across a table (applied force forward, friction back, gravity down, normal force up). Rules: arrows start on the object, point the way the force acts, and each has a name.

need: a tennis ball and a bat or stick

days.title: The normal force is not always your weight
days.goal: Measure the normal force changing as you jump, ride a lift or bounce, and find it can be bigger or smaller than your weight.

steps.title: Bathroom scale jumps
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: stand on a bathroom scale, squat fast, push up fast, and if possible ride a lift on the scale. Ask: 'When did the reading go above your weight? Below?' Say: 'The scale shows the normal force. Gravity on you never changed. When you push off, the floor pushes back harder than your weight, and that's what throws you upwards. When you run, your foot can push down with two or three times your weight.'

steps.title: Trampoline or springy bed
steps.do: If you have a trampoline, or a firm mattress on the floor, your child bounces. Ask: 'At the bottom of a bounce, which is bigger: gravity or the trampoline's push?' (The trampoline's: it is stretched and pushes back harder than your weight, so you go up.) 'At the top?' (Only gravity, so you come down.)

steps.title: Core worksheet: force diagrams
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Your child builds each force diagram, deciding which forces are bigger or equal, and explains the 'why' answers aloud before writing.

steps.title: Hidden forces at work
steps.do: Ask your child to find three normal forces and three applied forces in the room right now: the fan hanging on its hook (the hook pushes up), the chair under you, the wall holding a poster; a hand turning a tap, a foot on a pedal, a finger on a phone. Ask: 'Is there anything in this room with no normal force on it at all?' (Only things that are falling or flying.)

need: a lift if you have access to one

days.title: How much would you weigh on Jupiter?
days.goal: Calculate weight on other worlds, and find how gravity changes with distance and inside the Earth.

steps.title: Weight across the Solar System
steps.do: Do Activity a1: use your child's mass in kilograms and the newtons-per-kilogram table to work out their weight on the Moon, Mars, Earth and Jupiter, and how high they could jump on each. Ask: 'Did your mass change from world to world?' (No.) 'Why does Jupiter pull harder than the Earth?' (It has far more mass.)

steps.title: Twice as far, a quarter of the pull
steps.do: Hold a torch 20 cm from a wall and draw round the bright patch; then 40 cm away. Ask: 'How much bigger is the patch?' (About four times the area, so each part is a quarter as bright.) Say: 'Gravity spreads out the same way. Twice as far from the centre of the Earth, the pull is a quarter. Three times as far, a ninth. That's the inverse-square rule Robert Hooke suggested and Isaac Newton proved.' Ask: 'The Moon is about 60 Earth-radii away. How much weaker is the Earth's pull there?' (60 × 60 = 3,600 times weaker.)

steps.title: A journey to the centre of the Earth
steps.do: Ask: 'If you could dig a tunnel to the centre of the Earth and climb down it, would gravity get stronger or weaker?' Let them argue. Then say: 'At first it actually gets a little stronger, because the Earth's middle is so dense. But deeper still, more and more of the Earth is above you and around you, pulling you outwards in every direction. At the very centre all the pulls cancel, and gravity is zero: you would float.' Draw it. Then add: 'Gravity is a tiny bit weaker at the equator than at the poles, and on top of high mountains, and changes slightly over heavy rocks. Scientists map these differences from satellites.'

steps.title: Gravity sort
steps.do: Write on slips: Sun, Jupiter, Earth, Moon, an asteroid, a human, a grain of dust. Your child puts them in order of how strongly they would pull a ball held just above their surface (Sun, Jupiter, Earth, Moon, asteroid, human, dust). Ask: 'Where would a black hole go?' (Above everything, if it were heavy enough.)

days.title: Newton's cannonball and the falling Moon
days.goal: Explain orbits with Newton's thought experiment and a ball on a string.

steps.title: Newton's cannonball
steps.do: Draw a big circle for the Earth with a very tall mountain on top. Say: 'Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain above the air.' Draw a slow cannonball landing near the mountain, a faster one landing further away, a faster one landing halfway round. Ask: 'What if it went so fast that the Earth curved away under it as fast as it fell?' (It would never land; it would come all the way round.) Say: 'That's an orbit. Near the Earth you need about 7.8 km every second, which is about 28,000 km an hour. The space station does this, going round about 15 to 16 times a day.'

steps.title: Moon on a string
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: whirl a soft ball on a string threaded through a pen tube, with a small weight hanging below. Speed up and slow down and watch the circle change. Ask: 'What plays the part of gravity?' (The string.) 'What happens when you whirl slowly?' (The circle shrinks: not enough sideways speed.)

steps.title: Katherine Johnson checks the numbers
steps.do: Talk about voice v1, Katherine Johnson, who calculated orbits by hand. Ask the voice's question. Then say: 'If you go faster still, about 11.2 km every second near the Earth, you never come back. That's escape speed.'

steps.title: Orbit dance
steps.do: Your child is the Moon and you are the Earth, holding a dupatta between you. They walk sideways round you while you both keep the dupatta tight. Then you let go of your end: they walk off in a straight line. Then try it with them walking too slowly: they spiral in towards you. Put on slow music and dance it again: Earth turning on the spot, Moon going round, keeping the same face towards the Earth.

need: a soft ball in a sock, 1 m string, an empty pen tube, a small weight such as a bunch of keys

days.title: Satellites, and a spacecraft at a still point
days.goal: Find out what satellites do for us, meet India's missions, and see where a Lagrange point is.

steps.title: Satellites in your day
steps.do: Ask: 'Did a satellite help you today?' List together: the weather forecast (weather satellites such as India's INSAT series), TV and phone signals (communication satellites), maps and finding your way (navigation satellites, including India's own system NavIC), photos of crops, floods and forests (Earth-observation satellites). Ask: 'Are all these satellites falling?' (Yes, all the time, and missing.)

steps.title: Design a satellite
steps.do: Your child designs a satellite on paper for one job they choose: watching cyclones, counting trees, carrying phone calls to a village, or looking at Mars. They draw it with solar panels, an antenna and the instrument it needs, decide how high it orbits, and write one sentence on who it helps. Say: 'India's first satellite, Aryabhata, launched in 1975, was named after the astronomer who said the Earth spins. In 2014 India's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars on its first try, built by a team that included scientists such as Ritu Karidhal and Nandini Harinath.' Read the 'Mangalyaan team' perspective.

steps.title: The Sun–Earth still point
steps.do: Do Experiment e3: on the floor, the Sun is a big plate and the Earth a small coaster 2 m away. Your child finds a spot on the line between them, much nearer the Earth, where a spacecraft keeps pace with the Earth as it goes round. Walk it: Sun turns on the spot, Earth walks a circle, spacecraft walks a smaller circle staying in line. Say: 'In 2023 India launched Aditya-L1, a spacecraft to study the Sun. Since January 2024 it has been orbiting around the first Lagrange point, about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, where it can watch the Sun without ever being blocked by the Earth.'

steps.title: Who's falling?
steps.do: Ask true or false, and why: 'There is no gravity on the space station.' (False: about 90% of ground gravity.) 'A satellite needs its engine on all the time to stay up.' (False: once it's moving fast enough, it keeps falling round.) 'The Moon is a satellite.' (True: a natural one.) 'Aditya-L1 is held still by nothing at all.' (False: the Sun's and Earth's pulls, and its motion, balance there.)

need: a big plate, a coaster and a coin

days.title: The sea's two bulges
days.goal: Explain tides, spring and neap tides, and why the Moon always shows the same face.

steps.title: Tide table
steps.do: Find today's tide times for a coast near you (Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi, Visakhapatnam or Kolkata) in a newspaper or online. Ask: 'How many high tides today? How far apart?' (Two, a bit more than 12 hours apart.) 'Will tomorrow's be at the same time?' (About 50 minutes later.)

steps.title: Two bulges
steps.do: Do Activity a2: make the Earth from a ball wrapped in a stretchy cloth or a balloon. Your child is the Moon. Show that the Moon pulls the near side a little more than the middle, and the middle a little more than the far side, so the Earth is stretched into a slight egg shape with bulges on both sides. Then turn the Earth slowly: a sticker for your town passes through both bulges in a day. Ask: 'Why two high tides and not one?'

steps.title: Spring tides, neap tides and the locked Moon
steps.do: Draw the Sun, Earth and Moon in a line (new or full Moon): the Sun's pull adds to the Moon's, giving the biggest tides, called spring tides. Draw the Moon at a right angle (half Moon): the pulls partly cancel, giving small neap tides. Then say: 'The Earth's pull has slowed the Moon's spin until it turns once for each trip round us. That's why we always see the same face. And the Moon is drifting away from us by about 4 cm a year.' Ask: 'The solid ground also rises and falls by tens of centimetres twice a day. Why don't we notice?' (Everything round us rises too.)

steps.title: Dance of the tides
steps.do: Put on slow music. You are the Moon walking slowly round; your child is the sea, rising up on tiptoe with arms high when the Moon is in front or behind, and sinking low when the Moon is to the side. Then ask the 'fisherfolk' perspective's question.

need: a tide table for an Indian coast
a ball and a stretchy cloth or a balloon

days.title: Beyond Newton: curved space, bent light, slower clocks
days.goal: Go deeper into Einstein's idea and the evidence for it.

steps.title: The space blanket again
steps.do: Do Experiment e4, a harder version of the Class 3 blanket: roll marbles fast and slow past a heavy ball and try to make one orbit; then shine a torch beam 'path' along the sheet using a line of tiny beads to show how light's path bends near the dent. Ask: 'What does Einstein say gravity is?' (Mass bends space-time; things fall along the curve.) 'Which part of the blanket is wrong?' (Real space curves in all directions; the blanket needs Earth's gravity to dent.)

steps.title: Bent starlight and clocks that run slow
steps.do: Say: 'Einstein predicted that the Sun bends light from stars behind it. In 1919, during a total eclipse, astronomers photographed stars near the Sun and found them slightly shifted, as he predicted. He also predicted that time runs a little slower closer to a big mass. Clocks on GPS satellites, high above, run faster than clocks on the ground, by about 38 millionths of a second a day, counting their speed too. If engineers didn't correct for this, your map would go wrong by kilometres each day.' Ask: 'Would someone who lived at the bottom of a valley age more slowly than someone on a mountain?' (Yes, by an amount far too tiny to notice.)

steps.title: Ripples in space
steps.do: Talk about voice v4. Say: 'When two black holes spiral together, they shake space-time and send out ripples. In 2015 the LIGO detectors in the USA felt one stretch and squeeze the Earth by much less than the width of a proton.' If you can, play the LIGO 'chirp' sound online. Ask the voice's question. Then make your own chirp: hum a low note and slide it quickly up to a high one. Say: 'India is building its own detector, LIGO-India, in Maharashtra.'

steps.title: Draw space-time
steps.do: Your child draws a grid of squares like graph paper, then draws it again bending into a funnel around a star, with a line of light curving past it. Label: mass, curve, light.

need: a bedsheet, a heavy ball, marbles and tiny beads
a phone for the LIGO sound (optional)

days.title: What gravity tells us we can't see
days.goal: Meet dark matter and black holes, and weigh up a live debate.

steps.title: Vera Rubin's spinning galaxies
steps.do: Talk about voice v3. Spin a bucket of water with a few floating leaves, or draw a spiral galaxy. Say: 'In a galaxy, the outer stars should move slower than the inner ones, the way far planets go round the Sun slower. Vera Rubin measured them and found the outer stars going just as fast. Something unseen must be pulling them.' Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Chandrasekhar's limit
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, who at 19 worked out that a dying star above a certain mass cannot hold itself up against gravity. Ask the voice's question. Then say: 'A black hole is where so much mass is squeezed so small that not even light can climb out. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope team, using methods developed by scientists such as Katie Bouman, made the first picture of one's shadow.'

steps.title: Who Falls Into Whom?
steps.do: Play the founder's card game (g1). Players draw two element cards (Sun, Earth, Moon, Jupiter, black hole, a human floating in space, light, the ocean...), predict what gravity does between them, and check the outcome card.

need: a bucket of water and leaves (optional)
the printed Who Falls Into Whom? cards

days.title: Review and teach it back
days.goal: Bring it together: forces, weight, orbits, tides and curved space.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: weight on other worlds, orbits, satellites and tides.

steps.title: Challenge sheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 together, reasoning aloud. Choose three items if time is short and come back to the rest.

steps.title: Teach it back: Mission Control
steps.do: Your child is Mission Control and you are an astronaut. They brief you: what forces act on you on the launch pad (gravity, normal force), why you'll float in orbit (free fall), how fast you must go (about 7.8 km/s), what you'd weigh on the Moon, and why your clocks will run differently. Ask the check questions as a nervous astronaut. Finish with the project: show the satellite design and the solar system weight poster to the family.

need: the satellite design and weight poster

sections.p: A batter stands still at the crease. Show the two forces on him.
You push a book to the right across a table and it slides at a steady speed. Show all four forces.
sections.obj: a book pushed across a table at steady speed

sections.p: A lift starts moving up, fast. Show the forces on the person inside.
sections.obj: a person in a lift that is speeding up upwards

sections.p: A cricket ball flies through the air to the right after being hit. Show the forces on it (the bat is no longer touching it).
sections.obj: a cricket ball in flight, moving right

sections.p: Contact force or a force at a distance?
Match each force to an example.
You jump off a scale. Just as you push off, the scale reads…
The scale shows the ____ force, not gravity.
Why do you feel heavier for a moment when a lift starts going up?
Gravity can act without touching but the normal force can't. Why not? Think about atoms.
A 30 kg child. Fill in the weight on each world (weight = mass × N/kg).
On which world would the child's mass be smallest?
If you move twice as far from the centre of a planet, its pull becomes…
Match the satellite to its job.
Why doesn't the space station fall to the Earth?
opts: there is no gravity up there
its engines push it up all the time
it moves sideways so fast it keeps falling and missing

sections.p: A satellite is directly above the Earth in its orbit. Which way does gravity pull it?
When are tides biggest?
opts: when Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line

sections.p: Why is there a high tide on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon, too?
Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
An astronaut on the space station drops a pen and it floats next to her hand. A friend says 'there's no gravity there'. Write a better explanation.
Clocks on GPS satellites tick a tiny bit faster than ours. What would happen to your map app if engineers ignored this? What does it tell you about time?
Vera Rubin's galaxies spin too fast for the stars we can see. Give two possible explanations. What evidence could decide between them?
In a tunnel to the centre of the Earth, at the very centre gravity would be…
opts: the same as at the surface

sections.p: A trampoline jumper is at the very top of a bounce, not touching the trampoline. Show the force(s) on her.
sections.obj: a jumper at the top of a bounce

sections.p: Aditya-L1 sits between the Sun (to the left) and the Earth (to the right). Show the two pulls on it.
sections.obj: a spacecraft near the Sun–Earth Lagrange point

sections.p: Which piece of evidence supports Einstein's curved space-time?
opts: starlight bending near the Sun in the 1919 eclipse

sections.p: Why did the first two Indian astronomers' ideas about gravity not become 'Newton's law'?
opts: they were wrong that the Earth attracts things
they described the attraction but not a rule for how it changes with distance and mass

experiments.title: Bathroom scale jumps
experiments.question: Is the normal force always equal to your weight?
need: a bathroom scale (a dial scale shows changes best)
a lift, if you have access to one
a phone to film the dial in slow motion (optional)
steps: Stand still on the scale and write the reading: this equals your weight.
Squat down quickly. Watch the reading as you start to go down. Write what happens.
Push up quickly from the squat. Watch the reading. Write what happens.
If you can, stand on the scale in a lift. Watch the reading as the lift starts up, moves steadily and stops.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When you push up fast, will the reading go up, go down or stay the same?'
experiments.observe: The reading drops as you start to drop, rises above your weight as you push up, and in a lift rises when it starts up and falls when it starts down.
experiments.why: The scale shows the normal force: how hard it must push to support you. Gravity on you doesn't change. To speed up upwards, the floor must push harder than your weight (an unbalanced force upwards), so the reading rises. To start dropping, the floor pushes less than your weight, so it falls. In a lift moving at a steady speed, forces are balanced and the reading is your weight again.
experiments.safety: Squat and push up gently and hold on to something steady; step on and off the scale carefully. Don't jump on a glass scale.

experiments.title: Moon on a string
experiments.question: How does the speed of an orbit depend on the pull towards the centre?
need: a soft ball in an old sock
a small weight such as a bunch of keys
steps: Thread the string through the pen tube. Tie the sock-ball to the top end and the keys to the bottom end.
Outside, a grown-up holds the tube and whirls the ball in a flat circle above their head, letting the keys hang below.
Whirl faster: watch the ball's circle grow and the keys rise.
Whirl slower: watch the circle shrink and the keys drop.
Add more keys (a stronger 'gravity') and find how fast you must whirl to keep the same circle.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If we make gravity stronger with more keys, will the ball need to go faster or slower to keep the same circle?'
experiments.observe: Faster whirling makes a bigger circle; a heavier weight needs faster whirling for the same circle.
experiments.why: The hanging keys pull the string, playing the part of gravity pulling the Moon towards the Earth. The ball's sideways speed keeps it from being pulled straight in. For each size of circle there's a speed that balances the pull exactly. That's why satellites close to the Earth, where gravity is strong, must go fast (about 7.8 km/s), and the far-away Moon goes round much more slowly.
experiments.safety: Only a grown-up whirls, outside, with everyone at least 3 m away. Use a soft ball.

experiments.title: The Sun–Earth still point
experiments.question: Where could a spacecraft keep pace with the Earth while watching the Sun?
steps: Put the plate on the floor and the coaster 2 m away. Mark a coin spot on the line between them, very close to the Earth: about 2 cm from it on this scale.
One person is the Sun and turns slowly on the spot.
The Earth person walks a slow circle round the Sun.
The spacecraft person walks a smaller circle, always staying on the line between Sun and Earth.
Ask: who has to walk faster for their size of circle? Why might that work only at one special spot?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Would a spacecraft closer to the Sun normally go round faster or slower than the Earth?'
experiments.observe: The spacecraft keeps lined up with the Earth only if it goes round in exactly one year, even though its circle is smaller.
experiments.why: Normally, something orbiting closer to the Sun goes round faster. But at the first Lagrange point (L1), the Earth's pull outwards partly cancels the Sun's pull inwards, so a spacecraft there goes round in exactly one year and stays lined up with the Earth. Aditya-L1 orbits around this point, about 1.5 million km from us, which is about 1% of the way to the Sun. The still point is wobbly, so it needs small engine nudges now and then, like the Class 3 marble on the ridge.

experiments.title: The space blanket, harder
experiments.question: Can the blanket model show orbits and bending light?
need: a bedsheet held tight by four people
a string of tiny beads or a light chain
steps: Place the heavy ball in the middle of the tight sheet.
Roll marbles past it slowly, then fast, from the same starting line. Compare their paths.
Try to roll a marble sideways at just the right speed to circle the ball once or twice.
Lay the string of beads straight across the sheet near the dent, then let it settle: does it curve?
Discuss what the model shows well and what it gets wrong.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will a fast marble bend more or less than a slow one?'
experiments.observe: Slow marbles curve in and fall; fast ones bend a little and pass by; some circle before falling (friction makes them spiral in).
experiments.why: In Einstein's picture, mass curves space-time and everything, even light, moves along the curves. Fast things bend less because they spend less time near the mass. Real orbits last for ever because space has no friction; marbles on a sheet spiral in because the sheet rubs them. And the real curve is in all directions and includes time, which no sheet can show.
experiments.safety: Keep marbles away from very young children.

activities.title: Weight across the Solar System
steps: Write the pulls in newtons per kilogram: Moon 1.6, Mars 3.7, Earth 9.8, Jupiter 24.8 (at the cloud tops; Jupiter has no ground).
Weight = mass × N/kg. Work out your child's weight in newtons on each world.
Your child measures their best standing jump on Earth in cm. Estimate the jump on the Moon (about 6 times higher), Mars (about 2.6 times) and Jupiter (about 0.4 times).
Make a poster with a drawing of your child jumping on each world, and the numbers.
Add a line at the bottom: 'My mass everywhere: ___ kg.'
activities.outcome: A solar-system weight poster, and a child who can explain why weight changes from world to world but mass doesn't.

activities.title: Two bulges
need: a ball or round balloon (the Earth)
a stretchy cloth or a second balloon to stretch
a lamp or torch (the Sun, optional)
steps: Your child holds the Earth; you are the Moon, standing to one side.
Explain with three arrows drawn on paper: the Moon pulls the near side of the Earth most, the middle less, the far side least.
Gently stretch the balloon along the Earth–Moon line to show the egg shape: a bulge facing the Moon and a bulge on the far side, because the far side is pulled least and is 'left behind'.
Put the sticker on the Earth for your town. Spin the Earth slowly once (one day): count how many times the sticker passes through a bulge.
Move the Moon a little round its orbit and spin again: the bulges have moved, so tides come later each day.
activities.outcome: Your child can show with a model why most coasts get two high tides about every day, about 50 minutes later each day.

project.title: Mission Control briefing
steps: Finish the satellite design from Day 5: what it does, who it helps, how high it orbits.
Add a force diagram of the satellite in orbit (gravity only, towards the Earth).
Add the solar-system weight poster from Day 3.
Write a one-page briefing for an astronaut: forces on the launch pad, why they'll float, how fast they'll go, what they'd weigh on the Moon, and one thing scientists still don't know about gravity.
Present it to the family as Mission Control.
project.outcome: A satellite design, a weight poster and an astronaut briefing, presented to the family.

game.title: Who Falls Into Whom?
rules: Cut out the element cards and the outcome cards. Shuffle the element cards face down; lay the outcome cards face up.
On your turn, draw two element cards. Say what gravity does between them: who moves more, what happens when they meet, or what else you'd see.
Then find the outcome card that fits and read its back. If you were right, score 2 points; partly right, 1.
Anyone can challenge with a reason. If the group agrees the challenger is right, they get the point instead.
Most points when the element cards run out wins.

cards.back: huge mass; pulls everything in the Solar System
rocky, with solid ground
about a sixth of Earth's surface gravity
gas giant, no solid ground
so dense not even light escapes

cards.front: Element: a human floating in empty space
cards.back: tiny mass; keeps going straight
no rest mass, but has energy
liquid, free to flow
moving sideways at about 7.7 km/s

big: If gravity is curved space-time, is it really a force at all?
Is anything in the universe ever truly at rest?
If most of the matter in the universe is invisible, how sure can we be about anything we see?
Should space belong to everyone? Who decides where satellites go and what happens to old ones?
If time runs at different speeds in different places, whose time is the real time?

challenge.q: 'Astronauts float because there's no gravity in space.' Is that right?
challenge.hint: At the space station's height gravity is about 90% as strong as on the ground. The station and the astronauts are in free fall together, moving sideways at about 7.7 km/s so they keep missing the Earth. With no floor pushing on them, they feel weightless. There's no place in the universe where gravity is exactly zero, though far from everything it is extremely weak.

Everyone already knew things fall, and Indian astronomers such as Brahmagupta and Bhaskara II wrote that the Earth attracts bodies. Hooke suggested the inverse-square rule; Kepler had the laws of planetary orbits; Halley paid to publish Newton's book. Newton's genius was the mathematics showing one law explains falling apples, the Moon's orbit and the planets. Ask: what does 'discover' really mean?

Not exactly. Newton's law still works superbly for almost everything, including sending spacecraft to Mars. Einstein's theory gives the same answers in everyday conditions, but is more accurate near huge masses, at very high speeds and for very precise clocks. Ask: can an old idea be 'wrong' and still be useful?

perspectives.view: Fishing communities have always read the Moon and tides to decide when to go out and when the catch will be good, long before tide tables were printed. Ask: is this science? What would a scientist and a fisher learn from each other?

India's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars in September 2014, on its first attempt, for a small part of what most Mars missions cost. A photo of women scientists celebrating in saris went round the world. Ask: why did that photo surprise so many people? Who do you picture when you hear 'space scientist'?

The Moon has been falling round the Earth for about four and a half billion years, slowly drifting away, and has never once landed. It raises the seas and steadies the Earth's tilt. Ask: if the Moon could speak, would it say it is being pulled, or simply following its path?
Thousands of satellites and millions of bits of broken space junk now circle the Earth. Ask: who owns the space around the Earth? What should happen to a satellite when it stops working?

voices.idea: Johnson was a mathematician at NASA who calculated the paths of spacecraft by hand, using the mathematics of orbits. In 1962, before John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, he asked for her to check the new electronic computer's orbit calculations; she did, and he flew.
voices.then: She worked in a separate group of Black women mathematicians, called 'computers', who were kept apart from white staff by the segregation laws of the time and were rarely named on the reports they wrote.
voices.now: Her work, and the work of colleagues such as Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson, became widely known only with the 2016 book and film Hidden Figures. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015, and a NASA building is named after her.
voices.ask: An astronaut trusted Johnson's hand calculations with his life, yet for decades the public didn't know her name. Why do you think some people's work stays hidden? How could we find out who else did the work behind famous achievements?

voices.idea: In 1930, aged 19, on the ship from India to England to study, Chandrasekhar calculated that a dying star heavier than about 1.4 times the Sun's mass cannot hold itself up as a white dwarf: gravity would crush it further. This became known as the Chandrasekhar limit.
voices.then: In 1935 the famous astronomer Arthur Eddington publicly mocked the idea at a meeting in London, and many other astronomers followed Eddington.
voices.now: Chandrasekhar was right. Stars above the limit collapse into neutron stars or black holes. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory is named after him. He was the nephew of C.V. Raman.
voices.ask: A young student was right and a famous professor was wrong. How should we judge an idea: by who says it, or by the evidence? What would you do if a famous person laughed at your idea?

voices.who: Vera Rubin (1928–2016), USA, and Mordehai Milgrom (born 1946), Israel
voices.idea: In the 1970s Rubin, working with Kent Ford, measured how fast stars move in the outer parts of spiral galaxies. They moved far faster than the visible stars and gas could explain. Rubin argued there must be a great deal of invisible matter, now called dark matter. In 1983 Milgrom proposed instead that gravity itself behaves differently at very weak pulls (MOND, 'modified Newtonian dynamics').
voices.then: Earlier, Rubin had been told Princeton's graduate astronomy programme did not accept women. Her galaxy results were at first met with doubt.
voices.now: Most astronomers accept that some unseen mass is there, supported by other evidence such as gravitational lensing (mapped by scientists such as Priyamvada Natarajan). But nobody has detected a dark matter particle, and a minority of scientists still argue that gravity, not matter, needs changing. Rubin never received a Nobel Prize.
voices.ask: Is it more likely that there's invisible matter, or that our law of gravity is wrong at huge distances? What experiment would convince you either way?

voices.who: C.V. Vishveshwara (1938–2017), India, and the LIGO team, including Nergis Mavalvala (born 1968, Pakistan and USA)
voices.idea: In 1970 Vishveshwara showed mathematically that a disturbed black hole 'rings' at particular frequencies as it settles, like a struck bell (quasinormal modes). On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors in the USA recorded gravitational waves from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away. Mavalvala was among the experimental physicists whose work made the detectors sensitive enough.
voices.then: Einstein had predicted gravitational waves in 1916 but doubted they could ever be detected, they are so tiny.
voices.now: The detection was announced in 2016 and won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics for Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne, though more than a thousand scientists worked on it. The signal's final 'ringdown' matched the kind of ringing Vishveshwara described. A LIGO detector is being built in India.
voices.ask: More than a thousand people helped detect gravitational waves, but the Nobel Prize can go to at most three. Is that fair? How else could science give credit?

check.q: Name three forces on a book you push across a table, and say which act at a distance.
check.a: Applied force, friction, normal force, gravity; only gravity acts at a distance.

check.q: When can the normal force be bigger than your weight?
check.a: When you push off to jump, at the bottom of a trampoline bounce, or in a lift starting upwards.

check.q: A 30 kg child on the Moon: what is her mass and her weight?
How does a satellite stay in orbit?
check.a: Gravity pulls it towards the Earth while it moves sideways so fast that it keeps falling and missing.

check.q: What is a Lagrange point? Name a spacecraft at one.
check.a: A place where the pulls of two big bodies and orbital motion balance; Aditya-L1 orbits around the Sun–Earth L1 point.

check.q: Why are there two high tides a day?
check.a: The Moon pulls the near side of the Earth more and the far side less, stretching the seas into two bulges; the Earth turns through both.

check.q: Give one piece of evidence that gravity curves space-time.
check.a: Starlight bending near the Sun (1919 eclipse), GPS clock corrections, or gravitational waves (2015).

check.q: What did Vera Rubin's spinning galaxies show?
check.a: There is far more mass than we can see (dark matter), or our law of gravity needs changing; most scientists favour dark matter.

story.title: The Moon Is Falling Too
text: The year the rocket men came to Thumba, I was nine, and I hated them.

Our village sat on the sand between the coconut palms and the sea, south of Trivandrum, and in the middle of it stood our church, St Mary Magdalene, white against the blue. My father fished from a kattumaram, three logs lashed together, and my mother mended nets on the church steps with the other women, and their fingers flew so fast you could not see the knots being made. Then, in 1962, men came from the government with papers, and the bishop and the elders talked for a long time, and it was decided. The church and the land around it would be given to the scientists, for something called a rocket station. We would be given new houses further away.
"Why here?" I asked my mother, furious, while we packed our pots.

"Because of the Earth's magnet," she said, which made no sense to me then. Much later I learned it was true: Thumba lies almost exactly on the Earth's magnetic equator, and the scientists wanted to study the air above it.

The scientists were young men in white shirts and rubber chappals. They made their workshop in our church and their offices in the bishop's old house. They carried rocket parts on bicycles, along the same sandy lanes my father carried fish. I used to throw stones into the sea near the place where they were building the launch pad, as hard as I could, to show the rocket what I thought of it.
One evening a young scientist was sitting on an upturned boat, mending his bicycle chain, watching me.
"Good arm," he said.
"It always comes down," I said, crossly, as the stone splashed. "However hard I throw. Your rocket will come down too."
"It will," he agreed. "This rocket will go up higher than the air, higher than any bird, and then fall into the sea out there. Everything that goes up falls. Even the Moon."
I laughed at him. The Moon was rising at that very moment, huge and orange, out of the sea in the east. "The Moon is not falling," I said. "It's just there."

He put down his spanner. "Throw a stone again," he said. "Gently this time." I did; it landed close. "Harder." It landed further away. "Now imagine you could throw it so hard that it went further and further, so far that the Earth started curving away beneath it. The Earth is round, you know. Throw it fast enough, and by the time the stone has fallen a little, the ground has curved away a little. It keeps falling, and the ground keeps curving away. It falls all the way round the world and comes back to hit you on the back of the head."
I touched the back of my head without meaning to.
"That's what the Moon is doing," he said. "It's falling towards us, all the time, every night of your life. It's just moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing."

I didn't believe him. But that night I lay on the sand outside our new house and looked at the Moon for a long time, and I could almost feel it, the great white stone falling and missing, falling and missing, never landing, never leaving.

On the evening of the twenty-first of November 1963 the whole village came down to the beach to watch. There was a roar like a hundred storms and a streak of fire, and the rocket was gone before I could even shout at it. Then, a few minutes later, high, high up where the sky was still lit by a Sun that had already set for us, a cloud appeared, glowing orange like a marigold, spreading slowly across the sky. The scientists cheered. The old men crossed themselves. My mother put her hand on my shoulder.

"Sodium," said the young scientist, when I found him in the crowd. "Like the yellow in a street lamp. We let it out up there so we could watch how the high winds blow it. The rocket's already falling into the sea. Just as you said."
"Just as you said," I told him.
My mother was looking past the glowing cloud, out to sea, at the Moon. "High tide in an hour," she said, to nobody in particular. "It'll be a big one. Full Moon."
The young scientist turned round. "How do you know?"

She looked at him the way she looked at a badly mended net. "The Moon pulls the sea," she said. "Everybody knows that. When it's full, or new, the sea comes up higher. My mother taught me. Her mother taught her." She shrugged. "Your Moon is falling. Our sea is lifting. It's the same pull."

The young scientist was quiet for a moment. Then he laughed, and took a small notebook from his shirt pocket, and asked her to tell him about the tides, all of it, slowly. They sat on the upturned boat for an hour while the orange cloud faded, my mother talking and the scientist writing, and the sea came up the beach towards us, as she had said it would, and above us all the Moon went on falling, and falling, and missing.
story.epiphany: An orbit is falling sideways fast enough that the round Earth curves away beneath you: the Moon is falling all the time and always missing. The same gravity that holds the Moon in orbit pulls the sea into tides, which fisherfolk knew long before they read it in books. The turn is the young scientist's thrown-stone explanation, and then the mother's 'Your Moon is falling. Our sea is lifting. It's the same pull.' Underneath: the people who made way for India's space programme, and whose knowledge of the sea was older than any rocket. (The setting is real: India's first rocket was launched from Thumba on 21 November 1963, the scientists used the St Mary Magdalene church as a workshop, and early rockets released glowing sodium clouds. Mary, her mother and the young scientist are invented.)
ask: Why did the stone always come down? What would it take to make it 'fall all the way round'?
What did the scientist mean when he said the Moon is falling?
Why was Mary angry at the beginning? Was she right to be?
Who knew more about the Moon: the scientist or Mary's mother? Why did he take out his notebook?
What do you think happened to the families who moved? Whose names do we remember from Thumba, and whose do we forget?

ideas.idea: An orbit is a fall that never lands.
ideas.more: The Moon, the space station and every satellite are falling all the time. They move sideways so fast that the round Earth curves away beneath them. Newton's cannonball on a mountain shows it.

ideas.idea: What you feel as weight is the normal force, and it can change.
ideas.more: Gravity pulls you the same, but the push back from the floor goes up when you jump or a lift starts up, and drops to nothing when you fall freely. That's why astronauts feel weightless at 90% of ground gravity.
Einstein showed mass curves space and time; things fall along the curves, light bends, and clocks run slower nearer mass. GPS has to correct for it every day.

ideas.idea: Gravity reveals what we can't see.
ideas.more: Spinning galaxies, bent light and ripples in space tell us about dark matter and black holes we cannot see directly. Most of the matter in the universe seems to be invisible.

unknowns: What is dark matter? Gravity tells us it is there, about five times as much as ordinary matter, but nobody has ever caught a particle of it, and some scientists think gravity itself needs changing instead.

How do gravity and quantum physics fit together? Einstein's theory works for planets and galaxies; quantum physics works for atoms. Inside a black hole or at the very beginning of the universe they disagree, and nobody has a theory that joins them.

What happens inside a black hole? Einstein's equations predict a point of infinite density at the centre, which most physicists think means the theory breaks down there. Nobody knows what is really inside.
Is gravity a basic force at all, or does it emerge from something deeper, the way temperature emerges from moving atoms? Some physicists are exploring this; it is unproven.
